    Sprint 5 – Deployment, Optimization and Reliability

    📄

    Managing latency and cost for AI applications

    Lesson 2

    For LLM-based systems, user experience and unit economics have to go hand in hand. Our human brains are biologically wired to have specific thresholds on how we perceive latency: ~100 ms (instant), ~1 s (keeps focus), ~10 s (attention naturally drifts). This is why “perceived speed” tactics (e.g., streaming) are as important as raw throughput. You should build the applications to meet sub‑second TTFT for interactive experiences, and use progressive disclosure (like spinning progress wheels with notifiers about current actions being performed) for anything longer.


    In parallel, costs scale with tokens, context length and traffic shape. The margin your application can produce lives in design choices: prompt size, chunking, rerank cutoffs, cache hit rates, model routing, batch/offline processing and autoscaling policies. This lesson will provide few tactics about how to hit p95 latency targets and keep costs manageable while not sacrificing significant quality.



    What you should measure.


    Measure what users feel and how much you actually pay.


    Define the latency metrics you will operate on. For LLMs, three metrics are essential and orthogonal:


    • Time to First Token (TTFT) - time from request to the first generated token.

    • Time per Output Token (TPOT), also called inter‑token latency (ITL) - the cadence of tokens during streaming.

    • Total Latency (TTLT) - end‑to‑end from request to final token.


    TTFT is dominated by prefill (input processing), while TPOT reflects the steady‑state decode loop, both strongly influencing perceived responsiveness in streaming interfaces and should be tracked separately in dashboards and SLOs.


    Instrument cost and usage as metrics, not just logs. You should have token counts (input/output), cached tokens (when supported), and be able to analyze cost per request tied to model, prompt version, feature flag and user cohort. Two practical routes: 


    • Vendor‑reported usage in streaming (OpenAI exposes usage in the last SSE chunk when stream_options.include_usage=true - propagate this to metrics). This is the option we are implementing in the hands-on just without streaming.

    • Gateway/observability tooling that ingests costs for you (e.g. LangSmith native integration).


    Standardize the attribute schema so engineers don’t invent their own labels


    Set SLOs by UX thresholds and cost ceilings. A pragmatic starting point for interactive chat could be TTFT ≤ 300–700 ms, TPOT ≥ 6–10 t/s, and TTLT caps per feature (e.g., answers ≤ 5 s, tool‑heavy flows ≤ 8 s). Tie each SLO to a budget - max prompt tokens, max output tokens, max reranker candidates - so the system can enforce cost bounds under load without manual intervention. Keep p95 and p99 distinct, most of the techniques below are about dragging p99 down without affecting throughput.



    Latency and Cost optimization techniques.


    Streaming.


    Streaming simply means that we pipe the tokens as they are being generated in real time and show them to the user as soon as we receive them. Two numbers shape the experience: time to first word and the pace at which words appear. If the first words show up in under a second and keep arriving at a steady clip, the product feels responsive. Even if total generation time does not change, streaming improves perceived speed and reduces drop offs. Server‑Sent Events (SSE) are the simplest way to stream model deltas over HTTP.


    To make it work you usually have to:


    • Turn on the provider’s streaming option. Every major LLM API has a flag for this.

    • Have your backend forward the text to the browser as it arrives. Do not wait until the model finishes.

    • In the frontend, display chunks as they come in. Most web stacks can append incoming text to the UI without special libraries.


    Some additional recommendations:

    • Show a loading skeleton until the first words arrive, then switch to the streamed text.

    • Avoid long preambles in the answer. Get to the first sentence quickly.

    • If a slow tool call is needed, start streaming what you already know, then fill in the rest when the tool returns.



    Reducing Context size sent to LLMs.


    Cut prompt tokens. Do this by compressing rather than truncating. Long contexts raise prefill time and cost linearly at scale. Use prompt‑side compression to maintain important facts while reducing token count. Learned or rules-based compression can materially reduce input size while retaining answer quality, which directly improves TTFT and spend. In practice, codify compression as a transform (e.g., keep citations, strip boilerplate, compress repetitive sections) and measure the trade‑off by running evals.


    Retrieve less and better. Hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse) with a reranker typically improves relevance while letting you lower top_k and pass fewer/lighter chunks to the model. This reduces context tokens and consequently both latency and cost. Use a lightweight reranker or a managed one like Cohere Rerank between retrieval and generation.


    Use structured outputs. Don’t use free‑form text generation unless necessary. If the product only needs structured results. Use structured outputs (JSON Schema) or function/tool calling to make the model emit exactly the fields you need and stop early, this avoids long tails and retry loops due to schema errors. Keep a bound max_tokens, explicit stop sequences and where appropriate, low‑temperature settings to minimize randomness and creativity.



    Model choice and routing.


    Use cascades and routing to reserve expensive models for hard cases. A common, effective pattern is a 2-3 stage cascade: a small, cheap model handles the majority of requests, escalating to a larger model on uncertainty thresholds, safety triggers or failed validations (this is usually implemented by having a router node at the start of the agentic workflow). Productionize this with clear signals (answerability, retrieval coverage, toxicity flags) and log why escalations occur so you can push the boundary down over time. 


    You can also exploit inference tricks when you run the model. If you self‑host models, speculative decoding and related methods can reduce time per token substantially by drafting and verifying multiple tokens per step. These techniques come with nuances so you should measure end‑to‑end improvements on your hardware and prompts, speedups reported in papers often depend on decoding settings.



    Serving and inference layer.


    Choose a serving stack that matches your workload shape. For provider APIs you inherit their batching and scheduling, for self‑hosting, stacks like vLLM deliver state‑of‑the‑art throughput via PagedAttention (KV cache paging) and continuous batching (admitting/evicting requests mid‑decode). These techniques let you drive GPU utilization up without blocking long prompts behind long generations, improving both TPOT and capacity. Triton Inference Server offers dynamic and ragged batching, which is effective for stateless models and variable shapes. You should always tune queue delays and max batch sizes so the batcher doesn’t increase TTFT too much. Always benchmark with your real prompt length and output distribution.


    Budget and defend p99 with classic distributed‑systems tools. Long tails often come from a few blocked requests or unlucky stragglers. Use short, layered timeouts with retry + exponential backoff. For idempotent reads, consider hedged requests (issue a backup after a short delay and take the first winner). Apply these above the model call too (retrieval, rerankers, tools) so one slow dependency doesn’t bring down the whole interaction. Track and alert on p99 TTFT and per‑dependency timeouts so you can tell whether the tail is model‑bound or middleware‑bound.



    Caching and reuse.


    Semantic caching cuts both latency and token bills. Beyond exact‑match HTTP caching, cache semantically similar prompts and their answers using a vector store (e.g., Redis with RediSearch) and a similarity threshold. For many domains (FAQs, internal knowledge, templated workflows) hit rates are surprisingly high. Place the cache in front of the model call, return the cached answer instantly on hit, and record a “served from cache” metric so you can measure the benefit. Calibrate similarity thresholds carefully and tag cache entries with data versions so you don’t serve stale facts after a knowledge update.


    Leverage provider‑side prompt caching when available. Some providers cache the expensive prefill of repeated prefixes so you pay less and get faster TTFT for prompts that share large system instructions or context headers. This is near‑zero‑effort performance if your application naturally reuses big prompt prefixes across users or sessions, it also interacts nicely with structured outputs (stable schemas) and tool selection prompts. Measure whether your system actually benefits - if your prompts vary heavily per request, semantic caching at the app edge is usually higher leverage.


    At some point in time a technique called Cache Augmented Generation was making headlines (even though it was short lived). Here is a short description of a workflow that combines Cache Augmented Generation with Retrieval Augmented Generation:


    Data Preprocessing:


    1. We use only rarely changing data sources for Cache Augmented Generation. On top of the requirement of data changing rarely we should also think about which of the sources are often hit by relevant queries. Once we have this information, only then we pre-compute all of this selected data into a KV Cache of the LLM. Cache it in memory. This only needs to be done once, the following steps can be run multiple times without recomputing the initial cache.

    2. For RAG, if necessary, precompute and store vector embeddings in a compatible database to be searched later in step 4. Sometimes simpler data types are enough for RAG, a regular database might suffice.



    Query Path:


    We can now utilise the preprocessed data.


    1. Compose a prompt including user query and the system prompt with instructions on how cached context and retrieved external context should be used by the LLM.

    2. Embed a user query to be used for semantic search via vector DBs and query the context store to retrieve relevant data. If semantic search is not required, query other sources, like real time databases or web.

    3. Enrich the final prompt with external context retrieved in step 4.

    4. Return the final answer to the user.



    Batch where real‑time isn’t required.


    Move throughput‑heavy, low‑interactivity work to batch endpoints. Embedding large corpora, bulk summarization, audit/report generation, and nightly backfills shouldn’t compete for resources with interactive users. Providers offer batch jobs with relaxed SLAs and better economics (and often higher rate limits), such as OpenAI’s Batch API, while cloud platforms offer batch/managed endpoints for asynchronous prediction pipelines. Keep a “batch vs. live” switch in your code so features like “summarize this space” automatically route to batch when inputs exceed live limits.



    The TCO of LLM inference.


    One could argue that deploying and maintaining your own LLMs on an AI Cloud or on prem GPUs could be a challenge and brings its own additional cost - that is without a doubt true. The added cost however is usually fixed and linearly increasing with the amount of GPUs you will need. If you are running distributed workloads, the additional cost of operation (usually human labour) on top of pure GPU costs might be continuously decreasing when divided per GPUs operated.


    TCO (total cost of ownership) together with security requirements is an important measure that eventually should drive your decision of running with proprietary LLM APIs or serving your own models. When we think of the cost of proprietary LLM APIs it is all about input and output tokens. The curve of cost over time fluctuates with the traffic to your application.




    On the other hand, if you are deploying your own models on an AI Cloud, you will need a dedicated set of resources that are either always running or are shut down. In the simplest scenario, the cost curve over time is flat. Of course this is a rare case in a production application as you will want to implement some sort of autoscaling to bring your cost per token down and the users of your application happy with the responsiveness of the app.





    Throughput, latency and autoscaling in AI Clouds.


    The important part to evaluate is what kind of throughput and latency levels your application will require:


    • Throughput - how many requests per time interval the system can handle (usually measured in requests per second).

    • Latency - how fast the application is able to return the first relevant point of data. It is unique for LLM based applications, especially chatbots, as the first relevant point is usually considered to be the first returned inference token, the following tokens can be generated and rendered faster than an average human can read. The important measure here is TTFT - time to first token. So in order to reduce TTFT, we aim to reduce the time of Prefill.


    Not surprisingly, throughput can be increased and decreased by throwing more wood to the fire - increasing the size of your GPU cluster which is being used to serve the models. In some cases it is enough to scale the cluster horizontally, where the same model would be deployed on multiple machines to serve more traffic, in some cases there is a need to deploy the same model using more GPUs.




    In any case, it is worth pre-calculating the amount of GPUs you will need and do some estimation of the traffic that needs to be supported throughout the time - less traffic means less throughput needed. Knowing your approximate traffic needs, you can implement Upscaling and Downscaling strategies that would allow managing the TCO more efficiently.


    Additional advantage of running on an AI Cloud is that you would be able to control the throughput and latency to a granular level. This also means that in most cases, with enough tuning, you would be able to achieve lower latencies compared to when running with proprietary model API. Also, you can deploy other relevant services closer to models being served, reducing the end-to-end latency even more as the network traffic can be contained within a single region.


    An interesting stage in the process of building LLM apps is prototyping, this would mean no need to handle user traffic. While you can easily scale down to zero usage with proprietary APIs, you can also do that in AI Clouds by scaling the cluster size to zero during the periods of non-activity.



    TOC - Proprietary model APIs vs. Self-Hosting.


    Let’s see how the cost curves of Proprietary model APIs and AI Clouds could potentially look when overlayed on top of each other.




    The math is obvious. You are better off with an AI Cloud in green areas and you are better off with proprietary LLM API providers in the red areas. If you consider using an AI Cloud your goal should be to stay in the green as much as possible (when it comes to optimising TOC).
